label: rem:hkr-theorem
title: The Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem, and what it does not say at $q \neq 1$
html:
Let R be a commutative algebra over a field k of characteristic zero, and suppose R is smooth (for the reader who prefers geometry: R is the coordinate ring of a smooth affine variety, or the algebra of functions on a smooth manifold). The Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem [hkr-1962] identifies the Hochschild homology of R with its differential forms and the Hochschild cohomology with its polyvector fields:

  HH_n(R) \;\cong\; \Omega^{n}_{R/k}, \qquad HH^{n}(R) \;\cong\; \Lambda^{n} \operatorname{Der}_k(R),

where the first map sends the class of r_0 \otimes r_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes r_n to \tfrac{1}{n!}\, r_0\, dr_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge dr_n [loday-1998]. For a smooth projective curve M_0 the same statement holds sheaf by sheaf, and taking cohomology gives

  HH_n(M_0) \;=\; \bigoplus_{i} H^{i}\bigl(M_0, \Omega^{\,i+n}\bigr), \qquad
  HH^{n}(M_0) \;=\; \bigoplus_{i+j = n} H^{i}\bigl(M_0, \Lambda^{j} T M_0\bigr).

For a curve of genus g this reads: HH_0 = H^0(\mathcal{O}) \oplus H^1(\Omega^1) of dimension 2; HH_1 = H^0(\Omega^1) and HH_{-1} = H^1(\mathcal{O}), each of dimension g; and on the cohomology side HH^0 = k, HH^1 = H^1(\mathcal{O}) of dimension g, and HH^2 = H^1(TM_0) of dimension 3g - 3, the space of first-order deformations of the curve. The alternating sum of the homology is 2 - 2g, the Euler characteristic of the surface.

What the theorem does not say. Its hypotheses are commutativity, smoothness and characteristic zero. The classical limit obstruction is HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}), \mathrm{Ad}), the Hochschild cohomology of a noncommutative algebra at q \neq 1, and the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg theorem says nothing about it. The comparison arrow written as "HKR" in the Hochschild–Kummer connection is therefore not an instance of this theorem: it is an identification between a deformation-theoretic obstruction of the substrate and a gerbe-theoretic obstruction on the base that the axioms of a quantum observable universe do not supply. At q = 1 the algebra is the enveloping algebra of a semisimple Lie algebra, and Whitehead's lemmas make HH^2(\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g}), M) vanish for finite-dimensional M, so the obstruction space of the classical fibre is zero, not a line.

The closest statement in the literature is Kontsevich's formality theorem [kontsevich-2003]: for a smooth algebra the cohomological Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg map is the first term of a quasi-isomorphism of differential graded Lie algebras between polyvector fields and Hochschild cochains, which classifies the formal deformations of R in a parameter \hbar. That is the correct setting for a first-order comparison, and it is a setting the substrate parameter does not occupy: q - 1 \approx 0.11 is a real number at which everything is evaluated, not a formal variable in which everything is expanded. This is the fibre-versus-observable wall, and it is why the one-dimensionality of the obstruction space is stated as the Wigner axiom rather than derived.
